gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the 'single-cable' label hides two different video paths. Xebec's own help center says the Tri-Screen 3's one cable needs the separately sold Tri-Screen 3 Mac Adapter on every Mac, even one with Thunderbolt 3 or later ports. The Trio 3 Pro sends video over its two included cables, one per screen. Macworld's reviewer reports that its manual says no driver is needed on a laptop with two DisplayPort-enabled USB-C ports, while Macworld says plain M1 and M2 Macs and the MacBook Neo need Mobile Pixels' free software. Normalising each maker's '2K', 'QHD' and 'FHD' labels to pixels gives 3.14 MP per added screen on the Trio 3 Pro against 2.07 MP on the Tri-Screen 3, which is 52% more chart area per screen.
standout_why: I compared against these pages. Xebec's comparison page (cited) only says the Mac Adapter is needed 'for every MacBook Air/Pro'. It does not say this applies to Thunderbolt Macs too, and it does not say why. ChatGPT passed this on only as 'Mac users need an additional adapter'. Macworld's best-portable-monitors page (cited) lists the Trio 3 Pro as '2K (1920×1080)' in its spec box but calls it QHD in the text, and says only that plain M1/M2 and Neo Macs need software. Mobile Pixels' Xebec comparison page calls both products 'single-cable setup' without saying how the video gets there. deskgearhq says 'Single USB-C cable drives both panels' for the Trio 3 Pro and files it under 'No driver required', which differs from Macworld's two-cable test. itechguides 2026 never mentions Xebec, gives no driver or port rule for the Trio 3.0 Pro, and has no pixel-density comparison. The only rival text on driver-based video costs is generic: deskgearhq says DisplayLink 'can introduce compression, latency, CPU usage', without tying it to any product here. Partial pieces exist on rival pages, but none of them sets the video path and real pixel count side by side for each product.
decides: This supports the Trio 3 Pro as the pick for a day trader on a MacBook. On a Pro, Max, M4 or M5 MacBook with two DisplayPort-capable USB-C ports, both added screens run on the laptop's own video output with no adapter. Each screen has 2240×1400 pixels (187 ppi), and the Trio costs less than the Xebec today ($407.99 against $699). The Xebec Tri-Screen 3 drops for Mac users: on any Mac it needs an extra adapter that is sold separately, and each of its screens has a third fewer pixels. On a Windows laptop with a DisplayPort Alt Mode or Thunderbolt 3+ port, the Xebec runs from one cable with no adapter, so it fits that segment. On a plain M1 or M2 MacBook or a MacBook Neo, neither product gets both screens natively: the Trio needs Mobile Pixels' software. The table's footnote should state each row's video path and whether it needs one or two video-capable ports.
